fieldMarks: Relatively large, long-legged lizard (snout-vent 65-93 mm) with a flattened tail and long hind limbs.
Grey to brown back with yellow blotches and dark spots on both sides of the mid-dorsal line.
Tail and limbs have 4-8 dark cross bands, and the tail underside is boldly black and white striped.
Both sexes have a dark throat with radiating black lines; males also have sky to navy blue patches on each side of the belly, which females lack.
Males show metallic green-blue (sometimes orange and yellow) on the sides in breeding season.
behavior: Diurnal and heat-tolerant: often basks and is active in midday heat when other lizards shelter; most active about 0900-1300 in Nevada.
Wags and curls the black-and-white tail as a display to other lizards and when a predator is near.
Active in warm months and hibernates roughly October to April; digs burrows, usually under shrubs, for shelter and night retreats.
Eats mostly small invertebrates (ants, flies, spiders, scorpions), plus some plant material.
habitat: Open, sparsely vegetated desert with loose sandy soil: washes, dunes, floodplains and desert pavement, often among shrubs.
Uses boulders as basking perches and, at higher elevation, sometimes rocky shaded leaf-litter areas.
range: Deserts of the southwestern United States and northern Mexico: northwestern Nevada and southwestern Utah south through southeastern California, Arizona and extreme southwestern New Mexico to Baja California and Sinaloa; sea level to about 1,520 m. Not in Canada.
